summary: Specifies version 1 of RSVP, a protocol for reserving network resources for data flows, designed for an Internet with integrated services. Reservations are started by the receiver and work for both multicast and unicast. It was designed to scale well and recover from failures.

eli5.summary: It is like phoning ahead to reserve a lane on the highway for your video call. The person receiving the call does the asking.

questions: how does resource reservation work on the internet
what is soft state in rsvp
what is the difference between path and resv messages
subtitle: How receivers ask routers along a path to set aside bandwidth and other resources for a data flow, for unicast and multicast.

tldr.problem: An Internet with integrated services needs a way for applications to request specific qualities of service for particular data flows and have every router along the path set resources aside, even as multicast group membership and routes change.
tldr.mechanism: Senders send Path messages downstream to leave path state, and receivers send Resv messages upstream along the reverse path to request reservations. Routers merge requests, and the state is soft: it is refreshed periodically and times out if not.
tldr.outcome: RSVP version 1 is a Proposed Standard. It has been updated by several later RFCs, and it carries QoS and policy parameters without interpreting them.

today: RFC 2205 is a Proposed Standard published in September 1997, and it has been updated by RFC 2750, RFC 3936, RFC 4495, RFC 5946, RFC 6437 and RFC 6780. It has not been obsoleted, so read it together with those updates.

sections.title: What RSVP Is For
sections.content:
RSVP is a resource reservation setup protocol for an integrated services Internet. A host uses it to ask the network for a specific quality of service (QoS) for a particular data flow, and routers use it to carry that request to every node along the path and to set up and maintain the state needed to provide the service.

RSVP reserves resources for simplex flows, meaning one direction only, and it is receiver-oriented: the receiver of a flow starts and maintains the reservation. It sits where a transport protocol would in the stack, over IPv4 or IPv6, but it carries no application data. It is a control protocol, like ICMP, IGMP or routing protocols, and it is not a routing protocol itself. It consults the local routing database to find routes.

Making receivers responsible keeps the design workable for large groups, changing membership and receivers with different needs. A request travels only as far as the router where the receiver's data path joins the multicast distribution tree, so reservation overhead is in general logarithmic rather than linear in the number of receivers.
sections.eli5: RSVP is how someone listening to a broadcast tells the roads between them and the speaker to keep some room free. The listener asks, because the listener knows how much room they need.

sections.title: Sessions, Flowspecs and Filter Specs
sections.content:
An RSVP session is a data flow with a particular destination and transport protocol, identified by the triple (DestAddress, ProtocolId [, DstPort]). The destination address may be unicast or multicast. The basic protocol supports only UDP and TCP ports as the generalized port.

An elementary reservation request is a flowspec plus a filter spec, together called a flow descriptor. The flowspec says what QoS is wanted and sets parameters in the packet scheduler. The filter spec, with the session, says which packets get that QoS and sets parameters in the packet classifier. Packets in the session that match no filter spec are handled as best-effort traffic. The flowspec usually has a service class, an Rspec (the desired QoS) and a Tspec (a description of the traffic), and these are opaque to RSVP. The basic filter spec is deliberately simple: a sender IP address and optionally a UDP/TCP source port.

At each node, a request goes to admission control (are enough resources available?) and policy control (is this user allowed to reserve them?). If either fails, an error goes back to the receiver. If both succeed, the classifier and link-layer mechanism are configured, and the request is forwarded upstream.
sections.eli5: A flowspec says how much room you need on the road, and a filter spec says which cars get it. Before the road gives you a lane, it checks that there is room and that you are allowed.

sections.title: Reservation Styles and Merging
sections.content:
A reservation's style combines two choices. Reservations can be distinct for each sender or shared among senders, and sender selection can be an explicit list or a wildcard that selects all senders. This gives three styles: Wildcard-Filter (WF), Fixed-Filter (FF) and Shared-Explicit (SE). No style is defined for distinct reservations with wildcard selection.

Shared reservations suit applications where few sources transmit at once. The RFC gives packetized audio as an example, where each receiver might request twice the bandwidth of one sender to allow some over-speaking. The distinct FF style suits video. The styles cannot be merged with each other, because shared and distinct modes are fundamentally incompatible and mixing explicit with wildcard selection could give a receiver unexpected service. WF is kept alongside SE because a wildcard lets the classifier skip listing every sender, which costs less when the sender list is long.

When requests from different downstream branches meet at a node, they are merged and the largest is forwarded upstream. Since flowspecs are multi-dimensional and opaque to RSVP, the service-specific rules compute a least upper bound (LUB) when no flowspec is strictly larger.
sections.eli5: If a few people on a phone call never talk at the same time, one shared lane is enough for all of them. If everyone sends video at once, each one needs a lane of their own.

sections.title: Messages and Their Format
sections.content:
An RSVP message is a common header followed by a variable number of variable-length typed objects. There are seven message types. Receivers send Resv upstream and senders send Path downstream. PathErr and ResvErr report errors, PathTear and ResvTear remove state, and ResvConf confirms a reservation.

The common header holds a 4-bit version (1), 4 flag bits (none defined yet), an 8-bit message type, a 16-bit checksum (all zero means none was sent), the IP TTL the message was sent with (Send_TTL), and a 16-bit length in bytes. Each object has a one-word header with a 16-bit length (a multiple of 4, at least 4), a Class-Num and a C-Type. The maximum object content length is 65528 bytes.

Important object classes include SESSION, RSVP_HOP, TIME_VALUES, STYLE, FLOWSPEC, FILTER_SPEC, SENDER_TEMPLATE, SENDER_TSPEC, ADSPEC, ERROR_SPEC, POLICY_DATA, INTEGRITY, SCOPE and RESV_CONFIRM. The two high-order bits of Class-Num tell a node how to treat an unknown class: reject the whole message, ignore the object silently, or ignore it but forward it unchanged. An unknown C-Type for a known class should normally cause the whole message to be rejected with an error.

Messages travel as raw IP datagrams with protocol number 46. Path, PathTear and ResvConf must carry the Router Alert IP option (RFC 2113). Hosts that cannot do raw network I/O use the UDP encapsulation in Appendix C, with well-known ports 1698 and 1699. Each message must fit in one IP datagram.
sections.eli5: Every RSVP note starts with a small cover sheet saying what kind of note it is and how long it is. After that come labeled slips, and a router that does not know a slip's label follows the rule printed in the label for what to do with it.

sections.title: Path State, Soft State and Teardown
sections.content:
A sender periodically sends Path messages along the same route as its data. They carry a sender template, a sender Tspec and optionally an Adspec, and they store path state in each node, including the previous hop's address. Receivers then send Resv messages hop by hop along the exact reverse path, creating reservation state. In the host model, a receiver joins the group with IGMP, a sender starts sending Path messages, the receiver gets a Path message and starts sending Resv, and the sender then starts sending data.

All of this state is soft state. Path and Resv messages are refreshed periodically, and state is deleted if no refresh arrives before a cleanup timeout. Messages are plain IP datagrams with no reliability, so refreshes cover occasional loss. The refresh timer is randomized in the range [0.5R, 1.5R] to avoid synchronization, the lifetime must satisfy L >= (K + 0.5) * 1.5 * R, and the suggested defaults are R of 30 seconds and K of 3. State changes are forwarded immediately, but a change stops propagating where merging causes no change.

Teardown messages remove state at once. A PathTear travels downstream and a ResvTear travels upstream. The RFC recommends that end hosts send one when an application finishes, but a lost teardown is harmless because the state times out anyway.

Errors need care. If a merged request fails admission control upstream, the existing smaller reservation must stay in place. A ResvErr also creates blockade state, which makes a node leave the failing request out of the merge so a smaller request that would succeed can still be forwarded. A ResvConf is only a high-probability indication, not a guarantee, that a reservation is in place.
sections.eli5: RSVP keeps reminding the roads about your reservation every so often, like re-confirming a table at a restaurant. If the reminders stop, the table is given away on its own.

sections.title: Non-RSVP Routers and Evolution
sections.content:
RSVP cannot be deployed everywhere at once, so it must work when two RSVP routers are separated by a cloud of routers that do not support it. Path messages are sent with the data's own source and destination addresses, so they route correctly through such a cloud. A Path message carries the address of the last RSVP-capable router, and Resv messages are sent directly to it. RSVP passes a NonRSVP flag to traffic control, which reports the presence of such hops to receivers in Adspecs. A Logical Interface Handle (LIH) in the previous-hop information lets a Resv message attach to the right logical outgoing interface even if it arrives on another one.

The Class-Num rules let new object classes be introduced incrementally, and the RFC notes that forwarding unknown objects has scaling costs to be examined first. Error codes in Appendix B cover failures such as admission control failure, policy control failure, no path information for a Resv message, conflicting reservation style, unknown object class and traffic control errors.
sections.eli5: Not every town on the road has joined the reservation club yet. RSVP still works, but the towns that have not joined cannot promise anything, so RSVP warns the receiver about them.

sections.title: Security and Policy
sections.content:
The RFC's Security Considerations section simply points to Section 2.8. Corrupted or spoofed reservation requests could let unauthorized parties steal service or lock up network resources. To guard against this, RSVP defines hop-by-hop authentication with an INTEGRITY object using a keyed cryptographic digest, described in a companion document. The RFC notes that until a key management infrastructure for routers exists, manual key management is needed.

User authentication is expected to feed policy control, which decides whether a user may reserve resources, using POLICY_DATA objects that are opaque to RSVP. The RFC says their format and processing rules were still under development. For IPsec-protected data, where the transport headers are encrypted and ports cannot be seen, RFC 2207 defines an extension in which the IPsec SPI plays a role roughly like ports.
sections.eli5: Because a reservation can use up real network capacity, routers check that each request really comes from a neighbor they trust and from someone allowed to ask.
